Ammonia (NH 3 ) is a promising carbon-free fuel and a hydrogen carrier. In recent years, there has been a 
large number of experimental and numerical studies to understand the chemical kinetics of NH 3 in mod- 
erate to extremely complex systems. This study focused on understanding the chemical kinetics of NH 3 
in a simple system (pyrolysis). Shock-tube experiments were performed to monitor the NH 3 time history 
proﬁles during pyrolysis, with and without the presence of H 2 , using a new laser absorption diagnostic 
near 10.4 μm. The pyrolysis experiments were conducted for mixtures of ∼0.5% NH 3 /Ar and ∼0.42% 
NH 3 /2% H 2 /Ar behind reﬂected shock waves, near atmospheric pressure, and over a temperature range 
of 2100–3000 K. Using the data from the present study as a guide, along with NH 3 pyrolysis data from 
the literature, a detailed chemical kinetics mechanism for NH 3 pyrolysis is proposed herein. This mecha- 
nism was assembled using available reaction rate constants from the literature. The mechanism showed 
excellent agreement with the experimental results, as well as with the literature data. Additionally, an 
assessment of 15 detailed NH 3 chemical kinetics mechanisms on their capabilities of predicting the new 
pyrolysis experiments was performed. The assessment showed that these literature mechanisms yield 
signiﬁcantly different predictions, with only one model producing acceptable results for the majority of 
the NH 3 pyrolysis experiments. The effect of pyrolysis reactions on the prediction of oxidation data was 
investigated by updating the pyrolysis sub-mechanism of selected literature models with the reactions of 
the present pyrolysis model. The prediction of the updated literature models signiﬁcantly improved for 
ignition delay time and ﬂame speed literature data, indicating the importance of pyrolysis reactions for 
high-temperature oxidation chemistry.

1. Introduction 
Most of the electricity currently produced worldwide is com- 
ing from fossil fuel combustion, which increases the level of CO 2 
in the atmosphere and contributes to global warming. While large 
improvements in terms of CO 2 emissions have been made by pro- 
gressively transitioning power plants from coal to natural gas (NG), 
the ever-growing demand for energy makes it desirable (and an- 
ticipated in many areas of the world) that most of the increase in 
electricity production will be covered by renewable energies. 
However, most of the renewable sources of energy (solar, wind, 
tidal, etc.) are typically intermittent, which introduces a need for 
energy storage. While the storage of energy can be done un- 
der various forms such as batteries for direct electricity storage 
or pumped-storage hydropower to produce electricity on demand, 
only chemical energy storage appears to be both effective and af- 
fordable at grid-scale levels [ 1 , 2 ]. Chemical energy storage can be 
made in the form of hydrogen (H 2 ) production by water electroly-

It is also worth mentioning that since a large amount of hy- 
drogen would need to be produced, at an affordable cost, another 
(cheaper) way of producing H 2 without carbon emissions would 
be to use fossil fuels as a source but coupled with carbon cap- 
ture. Such types of H 2 production are thought to still be net- 
negative in terms of carbon emissions and have the advantage of 
possibly using various feedstocks such as biomass or even waste 
plastic. 
Regardless of the way it is produced, hydrogen is an extremely 
ﬂammable gas, and its economical storage and transport remain 
important, unsolved challenges [ 1 , 2 ]. These processes are also un- 
safe due to the very high ﬂammability and diffusivity of H 2 . A 
practical solution to these drawbacks can be found by convert- 
ing H 2 into a carbon-free, hydrogen-carrying fuel such as ammonia 
(NH 3 ) via a well-established industrial process [2] . Ammonia has a 
very low ﬂammability, is diﬃcult to ignite, and can be transported 
and stored in relatively low-pressure tanks, similar to propane 
[1] . These facts explain why ammonia has been considered as a 
hydrogen-carrying energy vector by many countries [ 1 , 2 ].

While producing hydrogen back from ammonia is possible, such 
an additional step would increase the cost and the energy spent 
during the whole process. The option of using ammonia directly as 
a fuel is thus being considered. However, the direct utilization of 
NH 3 as a fuel remains challenging due to its low ﬂammability. For 
example, the low reactivity of ammonia is problematic for gas tur- 
bines as it necessitates increasing the residence time by reducing 
the air ﬂow [ 1 , 3 ]. This workaround reduces the level of turbulence 
and therefore the effectiveness of the mixing and the eﬃciency 
of the combustion [4] . When compared to hydrocarbons, NH 3 ne- 
cessitates high temperatures to ignite in laboratory devices [5-7] , 
which translates into a high resistance to ignition in compression- 
ignition engines [ 8 , 9 ]. A recent review on the use of NH 3 in this 
type of engine [10] concluded that the implementation of ammo- 
nia in a single-fuel concept is challenging due to the extremely 
high compression ratios required. The aforementioned low burn- 
ing velocity of NH 3 , observed many times when measuring laminar 
fame speed in the laboratory [11-20] , is also not advantageous for 
spark-ignition engines, as it can induce large amounts of unburned 
fuel, combustion instabilities, and, potentially, knock. A few strate- 
gies have been tried to mitigate these drawbacks from NH 3 , such 
as very advanced injection timing [21] or various ignition methods 
[22] . However, as mentioned by Mounaïm-Rousselle and Brequigny 
[23] , a surprisingly small number of studies have been performed 
for NH 3 as a (single) fuel in engines. 
It is also worth mentioning that using ammonia as a single fuel 
can lead to signiﬁcant NO x emissions [ 1 , 2 , 24 ], which are regulated 
pollutants. However, post-treatment solutions or two-stage com- 
bustion [25] are possible for ﬁxed apparatuses like gas turbines, 
and NO x emissions similar or lower than with regular gasoline are 
observed for stoichiometric or slightly rich fuel/air mixtures in en- 
gines, with the fuel-lean cases being problematic [26] . Finally, it 
has been shown that a blend of hydrogen and ammonia possibly 
reduces NO x emissions to half of those from gasoline engines [27] . 
Thus, it is often considered that NH 3 should be mixed with fu- 
els such as H 2 [28-34] , syngas [30] , (a mixture mostly composed 
of CO and H 2 ), or natural gas (which can be biogas) [ 28 , 35-38 ]. 
However, while these studies with binary mixtures are of course 
necessary and important to facilitate the integration of ammonia 
into the energy mix, it must be kept in mind that the combustion 
chemistry of ammonia itself is still not very well known, as illus- 
trated by the ﬂurry of experimental and numerical studies carried 
out recently [ 5 , 39-44 ]. More speciﬁcally, a review of the recent lit- 
erature showed that while ignition delay time measurements are 
relatively well predicted by modern mechanisms, the same mecha- 
nisms do not provide acceptable predictions for any of the species 
measured in speciation studies [44] . Stagni et al. [43] concluded 
that “a comprehensive understanding of ammonia’s kinetic behav- 
ior is still an open challenge, especially below 1200 K and un- 
der diluted conditions”. This conclusion from Stagni et al. was also 
reached by a very recent study in a Jet Stirred Flow Reactor by 
Manna et al. [45] , where literature models failed to reproduce data 
for the oxidation of NH 3 . Interestingly, pyrolysis data were particu- 
larly poorly predicted in this study, indicating a need to revisit NH 3 
pyrolysis too. A recent study on ammonia combustion from Glar- 
borg et al. [42] showed that the largest uncertainties are present 
under low-temperature conditions, especially with high O 2 con- 
centrations, and that the experimental data under these operating 
conditions in support of proper model development are still very 
limited. Finally, note that most models also fail to predict accu- 
rately the laminar ﬂame speed of pure ammonia [46] . 
In the authors’ opinion, there are few if any other molecules 
for which such a large number of detailed kinetics models have 
been proposed within the past 5–6 years; picking what seems to 
be the best detailed kinetics model to design a combustion device 
running on NH 3 could be a diﬃcult task to start with. There is 
therefore a need for assessing the best models available in the lit- 
erature and for proposing new experiments and further validated 
models. This need for further model assessment can be illustrated 
by the results in Fig. 1 , where a proﬁle of NH 3 decomposition ob- 
tained during this study, for a simplistic NH 3 /Ar mixture, is com- 
pared to several detailed kinetics mechanisms from the literature 
[ 5 , 16 , 34 , 40-43 , 47-54 ]. The details behind the experimental mea- 
surement in Fig. 1 are provided in the subsequent section but one 
can see that the vast majority of the models cannot be considered 
as accurate, even for such a simple system. 
The aims of this paper were threefold. First, new experiments 
were conducted for NH 3 pyrolysis by following the evolution of the 
NH 3 concentration proﬁle with time via a laser absorption setup 
in a shock tube using mixtures of NH 3 and NH 3 /H 2 diluted in Ar. 
The second objective of this study was then to compare detailed 
kinetics models from the literature with the new data to assess 
the models’ accuracy. The ﬁnal objective of this study consisted 
of proposing a new detailed kinetics mechanism capable of accu- 
rately reproducing the present data as well as literature data for 
NH 3 pyrolysis. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study 
presents the ﬁrst shock-tube quantitative laser absorption specia- 
tion measurements of NH 3 at high temperatures. This paper starts 
by presenting the experimental apparatus and laser absorption di- 
agnostics, followed by a description of the developed NH 3 pyrolysis 
mechanism. The experimental results and numerical predictions of 
the new model are presented next, followed by a comparison be- 
tween the new model predictions and other literature data of NH 3 
pyrolysis. Finally, a comparison of the experimental data to the nu- 
merical predictions from the detailed chemical kinetics models of 
NH 3 from the literature is presented. 
2. Experimental methods 
2.1. Facilities 
Experiments to measure the NH 3 speciation proﬁles were con- 
ducted in a stainless-steel shock tube consisting of a 6.78-m long 
driven section and a 3.0-m long driver section with internal di- 
ameters of 16.2 cm and 7.62 cm, respectively. Polycarbonate di- 
aphragms with a thickness of 0.254 mm were used to separate the 
two sections. The driven section was vacuumed to a pressure of ∼
10 −5 Torr prior to each experiment using a combination of a me- 
chanical pump and a turbomolecular pump. Five piezoelectric pres- 
sure transducers, mounted along the last 2 m of the driven sec- 
tion, were used to monitor the propagation of the incident shock 
wave, thus allowing the determination of the incident-shock veloc- 
ities at four locations. These velocities are then used to extrapolate 
the incident-shock velocity ( v s ) to the endwall location. v s is then 
used in conjunction with the initial driven-section gas temperature 
(T 1 ) and pressure (P 1 ) to calculate the temperature (T 5 ) and pres- 
sure (P 5 ) behind the reﬂected shock wave (RSW). The estimated 
uncertainty in T 5 and P 5 are 0.8% and 1.0%, respectively [55] . 
Mixtures were prepared in a separate stainless-steel tank via 
the partial pressure method. The tank was vacuumed overnight 
prior to mixture preparation to reach a pressure of ∼10 −6 Torr. 
Three pressure measurement devices were used during mixture 
preparation with full-scale ranges of 0–1.333 kPa, 0–133.3 kPa 
(both MKS 626), and 0–1725 kPa (Setra 225). All gasses were 
supplied by Praxair with a purity level of 99.995% for NH 3 , and 
99.999% for H 2 and Ar. Before performing experiments, the mix- 
tures were allowed to mix for at least 1 hour. Two highly diluted 
mixtures, with and without the presence of H 2 , were utilized to 
study the kinetics of NH 3 in the shock tube. The two mixtures 
were initially prepared as 0.7% NH 3 /99.3% Ar and 0.7% NH 3 /2% 
H 2 /97.3% Ar. Although the same respective mixtures were used to 
ﬁll the driven section prior to each experiment, the mole fraction

2.2. Laser absorption diagnostics 
Measurements of NH 3 speciation proﬁles were obtained using 
a tunable quantum cascade laser (QCL) that generates narrow- 
linewidth light near 10.4 μm. The QCL was tuned to 957.839 cm −1 
to access the sQ(12,12) transition in the v 2 fundamental band of 
NH 3 —a transition that has been spectroscopically characterized in 
our previous work [56] . The generated light was split into inci- 
dent ( I 0 ) and transmitted ( I t ) beams using a ZnSn ﬂat beamsplitter. 
Two BaF 2 windows, located 1.6 cm from the endwall, were used to 
pass I t through the shock tube. The intensities of the beams were 
monitored via two, 1-MHz bandwidth, HgCdTe photovoltaic detec- 
tors (InfraRed Associates). Bandpass ﬁlters centered on 10,400 nm 
(FWHM 100 nm) and 10,177 nm (FWHM 708 nm) were used to 
cover the detectors receiving I t and I 0 , respectively. A ﬂip mirror 
was used to send the laser beam to a wavemeter (Bristol 671) to 
regularly monitor the frequency of the light.

2.3. Modeling of the shock-tube data 
All shock-tube modeling predictions were conducted using AN- 
SYS Chemkin software via a closed, homogeneous batch reac- 
tor model assuming constant internal energy and employing the 
volume-as-function-of-time (VTIM) method [60] . The non-ideal 
pressure variation during the experiments had a small effect on 
the modeling prediction of the NH 3 speciation proﬁles and was 
accounted for when performing the numerical simulations. Ac- 
counting for the non-ideal pressure variation was conducted by 
implementing a time-varying volume proﬁle V (t) derived from 
the experimental P (t) proﬁle by assuming an isentropic expan- 
sion/compression. The modeling predictions of NH 3 using the 
present mechanism (discussed next) with constant V and with 
V (t) are shown in Fig. 4 b to highlight the small effect of including 
the pressure variation when modeling the data herein. Modeling 
the data of the present study using Chemkin can be performed by 
specifying the pressure proﬁle as the extracted smooth-ﬁt experi- 
mental pressure proﬁles, which are included in the SM. More in- 
formation about modeling shock-tube speciation data can be found 
elsewhere [ 59 , 60 ].

3. Chemical kinetics model 
To the knowledge of the authors, the Davidson et al. [47] mech- 
anism was the only model speciﬁcally assembled for NH 3 pyrolysis 
and was only validated against experimental data from the same 
study. The present study used the Davidson et al. mechanism as a 
base model with four main stages of improvements. The ﬁrst stage 
of improvement was to add a few important NH 2 , NH, and N 2 H 2 
reactions that were not present in the Davidson et al. mechanism. 
The second stage was to add reactions involving N 2 H 3 , N 2 H 4 , and 
H 2 NN for the N 2 H x sub-mechanism. The selection of the added re- 
actions in the ﬁrst and second stage was guided by the pyroly- 
sis sub-mechanism of several modern detailed kinetics models of 
NH 3 . These reaction additions effectively led to an overall mech- 
anism that is generally consistent with the modern NH 3 mecha- 
nisms. The third was to adopt the thermochemical data reported 
by Bugler et al. [61] where they performed high-accuracy ab initio 
calculations to obtain accurate and consistent thermochemical pa- 
rameters for nitrogen-containing species. Finally, the fourth stage 
was to update individual reaction rates to best ﬁt the experimen- 
tal data reported herein, as well as the few pyrolysis data available 
in the literature. A survey of the reported reaction rates in the lit- 
erature was conducted, and multiple optimization iterations were 
performed to evaluate the effect of rate constant selection on the 
numerical prediction of the experimental ata. All the selected re- 
action rate constants were taken directly as reported in the litera- 
ture, and no tuning of individual reaction rates was performed. The 
proposed mechanism signiﬁcantly improved the predictions of the 
NH 3 speciation proﬁles provided in the present study and was vali- 
dated against the experimental data reported in the Davidson et al. 
study, and the few other sets of pyrolysis data reported in the lit- 
erature [ 45 , 62 , 63 ]. The proposed NH 3 pyrolysis mechanism, which 
is described in Table 1 , contains 13 species and 48 reactions, and 
the mechanism and thermodynamic data in Chemkin input format 
are provided in the SM. 
The model analysis showed that R4 −5 are the main NH 3 - 
consuming reactions which were both included in the Davidson 
et al. mechanism. The reaction rate of NH 3 + M ⇄NH 2 + H + M 
(R4) was directly adopted from the study of Davidson et al., who 
reanalyzed experimental data from four earlier studies to obtain 
a rate constant with lower uncertainty. Recently, Altinay et al. 
[77] measured the rate constant of R4 (in reverse) at low temper- 
ature using pulsed-laser photolysis of NH 3 . However, adopting the 
rate constant reported by Altinay et al. in the present mechanism 
signiﬁcantly accelerated the NH 3 consumption compared with the 
experimental proﬁles. It should be noted that Althinay et al. re- 
ported the rate of R4 with N 2 as a third-body collision partner, 
while the present data were obtained in highly diluted Ar mix- 
tures. Thus, a collision eﬃciency of Ar coupled with the Althi- 
nay et al. rate constant of R4 might improve the prediction of the 
present experiments. On the other hand, the Davidson et al. mech- 
anism employed a rate constant of NH 3 + H ⇄NH 2 + H 2 (-R5) 
from the Michael et al. [78] ﬂash photolysis shock-tube study. The 
present study adopted an updated rate constant for R5 from the 
study of Friedrichs and Wagner [66] , where they directly measured 
the reverse rate NH 2 + H 2 ⇄NH 3 + H (R5) using frequency mod- 
ulation spectroscopy in a shock tube. 
R6–13 are reactions of NH 2 with M, H, N, NH, and NH 2 . David- 
son et al. [47] measured the reaction rate of NH 2 + H ⇄NH + H 2 
(R7) to be 4.0 × 1013 exp( −3650/ RT ) in cm, mol, and s, with an 
uncertainty of 50%. However, the present mechanism utilized the 
reaction rate proposed by Miller and Bowman [68] for R7 (which 
is ∼70% higher than that measured by Davidson et al.). Although 
the selection of R7 had a minimal effect on the experimental NH 3 
consumption proﬁles, selecting the rate proposed by Miller and 
Bowman considerably improved the prediction of the experimen- 
tal NH 2 and NH peak data used during model validation (discussed 
later). All the reaction rates of NH 2 with NH or NH 2 were directly 
adopted from the theoretical calculations by Klippenstein et al. 
[70] except NH 2 + NH ⇄N 2 H 2 + H (R10) where the rate coeﬃ- 
cient provided by Davidson et al. [47] was adopted. R10 is the ma- 
jor pathway to form N 2 H 2 which plays a critical role in controlling 
the NH 3 consumption (as shown later in the chemical analysis). 
Selecting the rate of R10 proposed by Klippenstein et al. acceler- 
ated the NH 3 consumption, while the Davidson et al. rate of R10 
improved the prediction of the experimental data. 
R14–18 are reactions of NH with M, H, N, and NH. The present 
mechanism adopted the rate constant for the decomposition reac- 
tion of NH (and NH 2 ) measured by Deppe et al. [67] . The reaction 
NH + H ⇄H 2 + N (R15) is the most-promoting reaction of NH 3 
during pyrolysis at high temperature. R15 reported rate constants 
in the literature are limited, and the present study adopted the rate 
constant proposed by Miller and Bowman [68] . R19–22 are reac- 
tions of NNH with M, H, NH, and NH 2 . The rate constants for all 
these NNH reactions were adopted from the Miller and Bowman 
study except the dissociation reaction NNH + M ⇄N 2 + H + M 
(R19a-b). The present mechanism models this dissociation reaction 
per the recommendation of Nakamura et al. [40] who used the rate 
constant reported in Dean and Bozzelli [71] . 
R23–27 are N 2 H 2 dissociation and isomerization reactions and 
reactions with H, NH, and NH 2 . The rate constants of the N 2 H 2 dis- 
sociation and isomerization reactions to form NNH + H (R23) and 
H 2 NN (R24) were taken from Dean and Bozzelli [71] . Linder et al. 
[72] performed ab initio computation to determine the rate con- 
stant of N 2 H 2 reactions with H and NH 2 (R25 and R27). Chuang 
and Truhlar [79] also performed theoretical computations to deter- 
mine an improved rate constant of R25 by accounting for multi- 
dimensional tunneling. The present study chose the rate constants 
determined by Linder et al. due to the signiﬁcant deviation in nu- 
merical prediction of the NH 3 consumption rate (compared with 
the experimental measurements) when adopting the rate constant 
determined by Chuang and Truhlar. It should be noted that R25 is 
an important promoting reaction of NH 3 (discussed later). 
R28–36 and R37–43 are reactions of N 2 H 3 and N 2 H 4 , respec-

were the review of Dean and Bozzelli [71] and the study of Konnov 
and De Ruyck [73] . Additionally, the rate constant selection was 
guided by the study of Nakamura et al. [40] which validated the 
N 2 H x sub-mechanism in weak ﬂames where this sub-mechanism 
chemistry is important. An exception is the hydrazine decompo-

where the rate constant from Klippenstein et al. [70] was adopted 
due to its superior prediction of the N 2 H 4 data used in the mecha- 
nism validation (discussed later). Finally, H 2 NN is a major product 
of the NH 2 + NH 2 reaction (R13) at low temperature, and its reac- 
tions (R44–47) were adopted directly from the review of Dean and 
Bozzelli.

4.2. Model validation 
To assess the present mechanism performance against other 
data, a literature survey was performed to collect experimental 
NH 3 pyrolysis data. Generally, there is a limited number of exper- 
imental studies targeted to investigate NH 3 pyrolysis. To the au- 
thors’ knowledge, there are only four other studies where NH 3 py- 
rolysis kinetics data are reported. These studies along with their 
experimental details are summarized in Table 2 . 
Davidson et al. [47] performed shock-tube experiments to mea- 
sure NH 2 and NH proﬁles during pyrolysis of 0.01 −1% NH 3 in Ar. 
In their study, NH 2 and NH peak values as a function of tempera- 
ture for ﬁve different mixtures were provided. Fig. 9 shows a com- 
parison between the present numerical prediction and the David- 
son et al. data. The present mechanism shows excellent agreement 
with the NH 2 peak data of both mixtures for the entire range of 
temperatures. Additionally, the present mechanism well predicts 
the NH peak data for the low-temperature region (2200 −2900 K), 
while a small over prediction of the peaks is observed at higher 
temperatures ( > 3000 K). Note that in the Davidson et al. study, 
only an average pressure was provided for all the experiments, 
which was used to perform the simulations herein. 
Michel and Wagner [62] studied hydrazine pyrolysis in a shock 
tube for mixtures of 0.03 −0.5% N 2 H 4 in Ar. In their study, they 
reported N 2 H 4 half-life times as a function of temperature. The 
prediction of the present mechanism is compared with the N 2 H 4 
half-life times for two different mixtures in Fig. 10 . The present 
mechanism produces excellent agreement with the experimental 
data for both mixtures. It should be noted that sensitivity anal- 
ysis shows that at temperatures higher than ∼1300 K, the only 
sensitive reaction in determining the N 2 H 4 half-life times is R37 
(NH 2 + NH 2 + M ⇄N 2 H 4 + M). Multiple rate coeﬃcients for 
R37 are reported in the literature [ 66 , 73 , 74 , 80 ], yet the rate co- 
eﬃcient provided by Klippenstein et al. [70] produced the most- 
accurate prediction of the experiments. At temperatures lower than 
1300 K, R35 and R36 are important in accelerating the consump- 
tion of N 2 H 4 , and removing these two reactions yielded ∼50–80% 
longer N 2 H 4 half-life times compared with the experimental data. 
Recently, Benés et al. [63] measured NH 3 conversion and H 2 for- 
mation during NH 3 pyrolysis in a ﬂow reactor. Their experiments 
were performed for ∼0.1 −1.0% NH 3 in both Ar and N 2 in two 
types of reactors. Figure 11 shows a comparison of the numeri- 
cal prediction from the present mechanism with the results from 
Benés et al. for a mixture of 994 ppm NH 3 in Ar. The computa- 
tions were performed using the Chemkin plug-ﬂow reactor mod- 
ule by modeling the reactors with a ﬁxed temperature, using the 
experimental wall temperature measurements provided by Benés 
and coworkers. The NH 3 conversion data are well predicted by the 
present mechanism for the entire range of temperatures, while the 
present mechanism predicted accurately the H 2 concentration for 
temperatures below ∼1600 K. Above this temperature, the model 
slightly under predicts the H 2 formation, yet the predictions are 
very close ( ∼5% difference) considering the uncertainty of the 
measurements. It should be noted that modeling the ﬂow reac- 
tor data by ﬁxing the reactor temperature and using the residence 
time (2.3 −4.0 s) provided by Benés et al. yielded similar predic- 
tions at temperatures below ∼1500 K, but slightly under predicts 
(e.g. ∼10% at 1700 K) both experimental data at higher tempera- 
tures.

measured H 2 and N 2 concentrations for a reactor temperature

5. Conclusions 
The chemical kinetics of ammonia during pyrolysis was stud- 
ied experimentally by following NH 3 rate of consumption in a 
shock tube. A new quantitative laser absorption diagnostic was 
used to measure the mole fraction of NH 3 over a range of high- 
temperature conditions. Experiments to measure NH 3 speciation 
proﬁles were performed near atmospheric pressure for a tempera- 
ture range of 2100–3000 K in two types of mixtures: ∼0.5% NH 3 
in Ar and ∼0.42 NH 3 /2% H 2 in Ar. The experimental results were 
used as a target to assemble a new NH 3 pyrolysis mechanism. The 
numerical prediction of the new mechanism showed good agree- 
ment with the NH 3 speciation proﬁles. The new mechanism was 
validated against other experimental data of NH 3 pyrolysis avail- 
able in the literature. The numerical predictions of the new mech- 
anism were in good agreement with the available literature data, 
except for one data set, and a discussion of possible reasons for 
disagreement was included. Additionally, the performance of sev- 
eral detailed chemical kinetics mechanisms of NH 3 was examined 
against the experimental data of the present study. Overall, the 
chemical kinetics mechanisms from the literature failed to repro- 
duce the experimental data, especially for the NH 3 /Ar experiments. 
The exception was the model of Otomo et al. [52] which produced 
good overall agreement with the experimental data. Several de- 
tailed chemical kinetics models were used to investigate the ef- 
fect of updating the NH 3 pyrolysis sub-mechanism to the results 
of the present mechanism. The effect of the NH 3 pyrolysis sub- 
mechanism was examined for both pyrolysis and oxidation, and 
it was shown that NH 3 pyrolysis plays an important role during 
high-temperature oxidation. Based on its performance against the 
limited set of data available for NH 3 pyrolysis, the model pro- 
posed in the present study could constitute a base to build upon 
to develop and validate future NH 3 mechanisms in more complex 
systems.

The aims of this paper were threefold. First, new experiments were conducted for NH 3 pyrolysis by following the evolution of the NH 3 concentration proﬁle with time via a laser absorption setup in a shock tube using mixtures of NH 3 and NH 3 /H 2 diluted in Ar. The second objective of this study was then to compare detailed kinetics models from the literature with the new data to assess the models’ accuracy. The ﬁnal objective of this study consisted of proposing a new detailed kinetics mechanism capable of accu- rately reproducing the present data as well as literature data for NH 3 pyrolysis. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study presents the ﬁrst shock-tube quantitative laser absorption specia- tion measurements of NH 3 at high temperatures. This paper starts by presenting the experimental apparatus and laser absorption di- agnostics, followed by a description of the developed NH 3 pyrolysis mechanism. The experimental results and numerical predictions of the new model are presented next, followed by a comparison be- tween the new model predictions and other literature data of NH 3 pyrolysis. Finally, a comparison of the experimental data to the nu- merical predictions from the detailed chemical kinetics models of NH 3 from the literature is presented. 2. Experimental methods 2.1. Facilities Experiments to measure the NH 3 speciation proﬁles were con- ducted in a stainless-steel shock tube consisting of a 6.78-m long driven section and a 3.0-m long driver section with internal di- ameters of 16.2 cm and 7.62 cm, respectively. Polycarbonate di- aphragms with a thickness of 0.254 mm were used to separate the two sections. The driven section was vacuumed to a pressure of ∼ 10 −5 Torr prior to each experiment using a combination of a me- chanical pump and a turbomolecular pump. Five piezoelectric pres- sure transducers, mounted along the last 2 m of the driven sec- tion, were used to monitor the propagation of the incident shock wave, thus allowing the determination of the incident-shock veloc- ities at four locations. These velocities are then used to extrapolate the incident-shock velocity ( v s ) to the endwall location. v s is then used in conjunction with the initial driven-section gas temperature (T 1 ) and pressure (P 1 ) to calculate the temperature (T 5 ) and pres- sure (P 5 ) behind the reﬂected shock wave (RSW). The estimated uncertainty in T 5 and P 5 are 0.8% and 1.0%, respectively [55] . Mixtures were prepared in a separate stainless-steel tank via the partial pressure method. The tank was vacuumed overnight prior to mixture preparation to reach a pressure of ∼10 −6 Torr. Three pressure measurement devices were used during mixture preparation with full-scale ranges of 0–1.333 kPa, 0–133.3 kPa (both MKS 626), and 0–1725 kPa (Setra 225). All gasses were supplied by Praxair with a purity level of 99.995% for NH 3 , and 99.999% for H 2 and Ar. Before performing experiments, the mix- tures were allowed to mix for at least 1 hour. Two highly diluted mixtures, with and without the presence of H 2 , were utilized to study the kinetics of NH 3 in the shock tube. The two mixtures were initially prepared as 0.7% NH 3 /99.3% Ar and 0.7% NH 3 /2% H 2 /97.3% Ar. The model analysis showed that R4 −5 are the main NH 3 - consuming reactions which were both included in the Davidson et al. mechanism. The reaction rate of NH 3 + M ⇄NH 2 + H + M (R4) was directly adopted from the study of Davidson et al., who reanalyzed experimental data from four earlier studies to obtain a rate constant with lower uncertainty. Recently, Altinay et al. [77] measured the rate constant of R4 (in reverse) at low temper- ature using pulsed-laser photolysis of NH 3 . However, adopting the rate constant reported by Altinay et al. in the present mechanism signiﬁcantly accelerated the NH 3 consumption compared with the experimental proﬁles. It should be noted that Althinay et al. re- ported the rate of R4 with N 2 as a third-body collision partner, while the present data were obtained in highly diluted Ar mix- tures. Thus, a collision eﬃciency of Ar coupled with the Althi- nay et al. rate constant of R4 might improve the prediction of the present experiments. On the other hand, the Davidson et al. mech- anism employed a rate constant of NH 3 + H ⇄NH 2 + H 2 (-R5) from the Michael et al. [78] ﬂash photolysis shock-tube study. The present study adopted an updated rate constant for R5 from the study of Friedrichs and Wagner [66] , where they directly measured the reverse rate NH 2 + H 2 ⇄NH 3 + H (R5) using frequency mod- ulation spectroscopy in a shock tube. R6–13 are reactions of NH 2 with M, H, N, NH, and NH 2 . David- son et al. [47] measured the reaction rate of NH 2 + H ⇄NH + H 2 (R7) to be 4.0 × 1013 exp( −3650/ RT ) in cm, mol, and s, with an uncertainty of 50%. However, the present mechanism utilized the reaction rate proposed by Miller and Bowman [68] for R7 (which is ∼70% higher than that measured by Davidson et al.). Although the selection of R7 had a minimal effect on the experimental NH 3 consumption proﬁles, selecting the rate proposed by Miller and Bowman considerably improved the prediction of the experimen- tal NH 2 and NH peak data used during model validation (discussed later). All the reaction rates of NH 2 with NH or NH 2 were directly adopted from the theoretical calculations by Klippenstein et al. [70] except NH 2 + NH ⇄N 2 H 2 + H (R10) where the rate coeﬃ- cient provided by Davidson et al. [47] was adopted. R10 is the ma- jor pathway to form N 2 H 2 which plays a critical role in controlling the NH 3 consumption (as shown later in the chemical analysis). Selecting the rate of R10 proposed by Klippenstein et al. acceler- ated the NH 3 consumption, while the Davidson et al. rate of R10 improved the prediction of the experimental data. R14–18 are reactions of NH with M, H, N, and NH. The present mechanism adopted the rate constant for the decomposition reac- tion of NH (and NH 2 ) measured by Deppe et al. [67] . The reaction NH + H ⇄H 2 + N (R15) is the most-promoting reaction of NH 3 during pyrolysis at high temperature. R15 reported rate constants in the literature are limited, and the present study adopted the rate constant proposed by Miller and Bowman [68] . R19–22 are reac- tions of NNH with M, H, NH, and NH 2 . The rate constants for all these NNH reactions were adopted from the Miller and Bowman study except the dissociation reaction NNH + M ⇄N 2 + H + M (R19a-b). The present mechanism models this dissociation reaction per the recommendation of Nakamura et al. [40] who used the rate constant reported in Dean and Bozzelli [71] . R23–27 are N 2 H 2 dissociation and isomerization reactions and reactions with H, NH, and NH 2 . The rate constants of the N 2 H 2 dis- sociation and isomerization reactions to form NNH + H (R23) and H 2 NN (R24) were taken from Dean and Bozzelli [71] . Linder et al. [72] performed ab initio computation to determine the rate con- stant of N 2 H 2 reactions with H and NH 2 (R25 and R27). Chuang and Truhlar [79] also performed theoretical computations to deter- mine an improved rate constant of R25 by accounting for multi- dimensional tunneling. The present study chose the rate constants determined by Linder et al. due to the signiﬁcant deviation in nu- merical prediction of the NH 3 consumption rate (compared with the experimental measurements) when adopting the rate constant determined by Chuang and Truhlar. It should be noted that R25 is an important promoting reaction of NH 3 (discussed later). R28–36 and R37–43 are reactions of N 2 H 3 and N 2 H 4 , respec- tively. The major sources of the rate constant of these reactions were the review of Dean and Bozzelli [71] and the study of Konnov and De Ruyck [73] . Additionally, the rate constant selection was guided by the study of Nakamura et al. [40] which validated the N 2 H x sub-mechanism in weak ﬂames where this sub-mechanism chemistry is important. An exception is the hydrazine decompo- sition reaction N 2 H 4 + M ⇄NH 2 + NH 2 + M (R37 in reverse) where the rate constant from Klippenstein et al. [70] was adopted due to its superior prediction of the N 2 H 4 data used in the mecha- nism validation (discussed later). Finally, H 2 NN is a major product of the NH 2 + NH 2 reaction (R13) at low temperature, and its reac- tions (R44–47) were adopted directly from the review of Dean and Bozzelli. 4. Conclusions The chemical kinetics of ammonia during pyrolysis was stud- ied experimentally by following NH 3 rate of consumption in a shock tube. A new quantitative laser absorption diagnostic was used to measure the mole fraction of NH 3 over a range of high- temperature conditions. Experiments to measure NH 3 speciation proﬁles were performed near atmospheric pressure for a tempera- ture range of 2100–3000 K in two types of mixtures: ∼0.5% NH 3 in Ar and ∼0.42 NH 3 /2% H 2 in Ar. The experimental results were used as a target to assemble a new NH 3 pyrolysis mechanism. The numerical prediction of the new mechanism showed good agree- ment with the NH 3 speciation proﬁles. The new mechanism was validated against other experimental data of NH 3 pyrolysis avail- able in the literature. The numerical predictions of the new mech- anism were in good agreement with the available literature data, except for one data set, and a discussion of possible reasons for disagreement was included. Additionally, the performance of sev- eral detailed chemical kinetics mechanisms of NH 3 was examined against the experimental data of the present study. Overall, the chemical kinetics mechanisms from the literature failed to repro- duce the experimental data, especially for the NH 3 /Ar experiments. The exception was the model of Otomo et al. [52] which produced good overall agreement with the experimental data. Several de- tailed chemical kinetics models were used to investigate the ef- fect of updating the NH 3 pyrolysis sub-mechanism to the results of the present mechanism. The effect of the NH 3 pyrolysis sub- mechanism was examined for both pyrolysis and oxidation, and it was shown that NH 3 pyrolysis plays an important role during high-temperature oxidation. Based on its performance against the limited set of data available for NH 3 pyrolysis, the model pro- posed in the present study could constitute a base to build upon to develop and validate future NH 3 mechanisms in more complex systems.
